stem: Which is an example of **work in progress**?

options.content: Chairs that have been assembled but not yet varnished
options.rationale: Correct: partly finished goods.

options.content: Planks of timber waiting in the yard
options.rationale: These are raw materials.

options.content: Varnished chairs packed and ready to deliver
options.rationale: These are finished goods.

options.content: Money owed by customers for chairs
options.rationale: That is trade receivables, not inventory.

explanation: Work in progress is partly made goods still in production.

options.content: The time between ordering goods and receiving them
options.rationale: Correct: the delivery waiting time.

options.content: The time it takes to sell all the finished goods
options.rationale: That relates to stock turnover.

options.content: The time workers take to make one product
options.rationale: That is production time.

options.content: The time allowed to pay a supplier's invoice
options.rationale: That is the credit period.

explanation: Lead time is the delay between placing an order and the goods arriving.

stem: Which is a **cost** of holding a large amount of inventory?

options.content: Production may stop because materials run out
options.rationale: That is a cost of holding too little inventory.

options.content: Customers may go to rivals because goods are unavailable
options.rationale: That is a cost of holding too little.

options.content: Bulk-buying discounts are lost
options.rationale: Holding more stock usually gains bulk discounts.

options.content: Cash is tied up that could be used elsewhere
options.rationale: Correct: money spent on stock is not available for other uses.

explanation: Large inventories tie up working capital and cost money to store, insure and protect.

stem: Why does a business keep a buffer stock?

options.content: To make sure it never has to buy from suppliers again
options.rationale: Buffer stock is used up and must be replaced.

options.content: To keep going if a delivery is late or demand rises suddenly
options.rationale: Correct: buffer stock is a safety margin.

options.content: To increase the amount of cash in the bank
options.rationale: Holding stock uses cash.

options.content: To avoid paying for storage space
options.rationale: Buffer stock needs storage space.

explanation: Buffer (safety) stock protects against delays and unexpected demand.

stem: Ordering school-uniform fabric in October so that it arrives before the January rush meets which right of purchasing?

options.content: Right quality
options.rationale: Quality is about fitness for purpose.

options.content: Right source
options.rationale: Source is about choosing a reliable supplier.

options.content: Right time
options.rationale: Correct: goods arrive when they are needed.

options.content: Right price
options.rationale: Price is about best value.

explanation: Allowing for lead time so goods arrive when needed is the right time.

stem: Which business is likely to hold the **smallest** inventory compared with its sales?

options.content: A hardware shop selling tools and cement
options.rationale: Hardware keeps well and many lines are stocked.

options.content: A car-parts importer with long lead times
options.rationale: Long, uncertain lead times need large stocks.

options.content: A furniture showroom displaying many designs
options.rationale: Showrooms hold stock for display and choice.

options.content: A bakery selling fresh bread daily
options.rationale: Correct: bread is perishable and made daily.

explanation: Perishable goods cannot be stored for long, so inventory is kept low.

stem: A manufacturer imports its main component and deliveries are often delayed at the border. What should it do with its inventory?

options.content: Hold no stock at all and order daily
options.rationale: With unreliable deliveries production would often stop.

options.content: Stop production whenever a delivery is late
options.rationale: This loses sales and wastes labour.

options.content: Hold a larger buffer stock of the component
options.rationale: Correct: protects production against delays.

options.content: Sell its finished goods only on credit
options.rationale: Credit terms do not solve supply delays.

explanation: Long or uncertain lead times call for more safety stock, despite the cost.
hints: What protects production when supplies are uncertain?

stem: In the purchasing cycle, what happens **immediately after** quotations are compared?

options.content: The goods are received and checked
options.rationale: Goods arrive only after an order is placed.

options.content: The supplier is chosen and an order is placed
options.rationale: Correct: comparison leads to choosing a supplier.

options.content: The supplier's invoice is paid
options.rationale: Payment comes after the goods and invoice arrive.

options.content: The need for materials is identified
options.rationale: This is the first step of the cycle.

explanation: Need → find suppliers → quotations → choose and order → receive and check → pay → review.

stem: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods are all types of inventory.
explanation: True. These are the three types of inventory a manufacturer holds.

stem: The best supplier is always the one with the lowest price per unit.
explanation: False. Delivery costs, quality, reliability, lead time and credit terms all matter (the five rights).

stem: Match each right of purchasing with its meaning.

right.content: Best value including discounts and delivery
Goods arrive when they are needed
A reliable supplier with good service
Enough to meet needs without overstocking

explanation: The five rights guide every buying decision.

payload.template: Inventory kept in case of late deliveries is called {{blank:a}} stock. Buying from suppliers using the internet and electronic payments is called {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Buffer stock is a safety margin; e-purchasing is electronic buying.

stem: A paint maker needs 800 litres of resin. Supplier X charges US\$2.60 a litre plus US\$120 delivery. Supplier Y charges US\$2.45 a litre plus US\$290 delivery. Calculate how much cheaper Supplier X is in total.

A shoe factory uses 45 m² of leather a day. The supplier's lead time is 6 days and the factory keeps a buffer stock of 90 m². At what stock level (in m²) should it re-order so that it does not fall below the buffer stock?
explanation: Used during the lead time = 45 × 6 = 270; re-order level = 270 + 90 = 360 m².
workedSolution: 1. Used during the lead time = 45 × 6 = 270; re-order level = 270 + 90 = 360 m².
hints: How much is used while waiting for delivery?

stem: A wholesaler holds inventory worth US\$18,000 on average. Assume the yearly cost of storing, insuring and financing it is 20% of its value. Calculate the yearly cost of holding the inventory.
Explain **two** reasons why a manufacturer holds inventory of raw materials.

points.description: Reason 1, e.g. production continues if delivery is late (1)
Explained: workers and machines are not left idle; orders met (1)
Reason 2, e.g. bulk-buying discounts / meet sudden rise in demand / expected price rises (1)
Explained: lower cost per unit / sales not lost (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Holding raw materials keeps production going if a supplier delivers late, so workers and machines are not idle. Buying in larger quantities also gains bulk-buying discounts, which lowers the cost of each unit produced.

explanation: Inventory protects production and can reduce costs.
hints: What happens if materials run out?

stem: Explain **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of e-purchasing for a small enterprise.

points.description: Advantage, e.g. compare many suppliers' prices quickly (1)
Explained: lower costs / time saved / orders at any time (1)
Disadvantage, e.g. fraud risk / cannot inspect goods / needs internet and power (1)
Explained: may lose money or receive poor-quality goods / orders fail during outages (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: E-purchasing lets the owner compare the prices of many suppliers quickly online, so materials can be bought more cheaply. However, the goods cannot be inspected before buying, so the enterprise may receive poor-quality materials or be cheated by a fake website.

explanation: E-purchasing is fast and cheap but carries fraud and quality risks.
hints: Think about price comparison and about trust.

stem:
Rudo runs a poultry farm near Chinhoyi. She needs 400 bags of chicken feed a month and has received two quotations.

| Supplier | Price per bag (US\$) | Delivery charge (US\$) | Lead time | Quality | Credit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| Kudzai Feeds (Harare) | 14.50 | 150 | 2 days | Good | 30 days |
| Mvura Agro (Bulawayo) | 13.80 | 420 | 7 days | Good | Cash only |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total monthly cost of buying from Kudzai Feeds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total monthly cost of buying from Mvura Agro.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** of the five rights of purchasing, other than price, that Rudo should consider.

points.description: Right time (lead time) (1)
Right quality / right source / right quantity (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Recommend which supplier Rudo should choose. Justify your answer.

points.description: Total cost: Mvura cheaper by US\$10 a month (1)
Kudzai: 2-day lead time, less buffer stock needed; chickens must be fed every day (1)
Kudzai gives 30 days' credit: helps cash flow (1)
Mvura: cash only and 7-day lead time: more stock and cash tied up (1)
Quality is equal, so other factors decide (1)
Justified recommendation (1)

explanation: Kudzai US\$5,950; Mvura US\$5,940. The saving must be weighed against lead time and credit.

stem: Nyasha owns a clothing shop in Gweru. She holds inventory worth US\$36,000 and sells about US\$12,000 of stock (at cost) a month. Many dresses have been in the shop for over six months. She is short of cash to pay her rent.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate how many months of sales her inventory would last.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain **two** costs to Nyasha of holding this much inventory.

points.description: Cash tied up: cannot pay rent (1)
Developed: may need an overdraft and pay interest (1)
Goods go out of fashion / damaged / storage and insurance costs (1)
Developed: may have to sell at a loss later (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Recommend how Nyasha should manage her inventory in future. Justify your answer.

points.description: Clearance sale of old dresses to raise cash (1)
Buy smaller quantities more often; watch which lines sell (1)
Keep stock records / set maximum levels (1)
Justified, with drawback (lower margins, more orders) (1)

explanation: Inventory covers 3 months of sales: too much cash tied up in slow-moving stock.
hints: Divide the inventory by monthly sales.
